summary:
Planning a mission near the Moon's south pole is challenging because sunlight, terrain and Earth visibility can vary significantly between locations and dates. These conditions affect solar power availability, communications and mission scheduling.

Lunar Mission Navigator is an interactive mission-planning platform developed to make these complex environmental conditions easier to explore and compare.

Our platform features a 3D Moon that allows users to explore six south-polar locations, examine terrain conditions, select mission dates and compare estimated sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility. Using NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter terrain data and JPL Horizons ephemeris data, the system calculates potential operating windows and presents the results through interactive charts, mission timelines and downloadable mission briefs.

Unlike traditional static maps, our platform combines lunar exploration, environmental analysis and mission planning in one accessible interface.

Our goal is to make lunar mission-planning concepts easier to understand for students, researchers and space enthusiasts while demonstrating how publicly available NASA data can support informed exploration. The results are educational estimates rather than validated mission forecasts.
details:
Project Overview

Lunar Mission Navigator is an interactive, web-based platform designed to help users explore and compare potential lunar mission locations near the Moon's south pole. Our project addresses the challenge of understanding how terrain, sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility influence the suitability of different locations and operating periods.

The Moon's south pole is particularly interesting for future exploration because its unusual lighting conditions and complex terrain create both opportunities and operational challenges. We wanted to transform publicly available scientific datasets into an accessible experience that allows users to explore these factors without requiring specialised mission-planning software.

How Our Project Works

Our platform combines interactive 3D visualisation, lunar terrain information and environmental calculations into a single mission-planning experience.

1. Interactive 3D Lunar Explorer

Users can explore a textured 3D Moon, rotate the lunar globe, zoom into the south-polar region and select locations for further analysis. The visualisation includes terrain and lunar imagery derived from NASA resources.

2. Landing-Site Comparison

The platform allows users to investigate six south-polar locations, including Shackleton, de Gerlache, Malapert, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1 and Haworth. Users can compare the environmental conditions associated with these locations to better understand their potential advantages and limitations.

3. Sunlight and Earth Visibility Analysis

Using NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter terrain data and JPL Horizons ephemeris data, the application estimates when sunlight and Earth are visible from a selected location.

Our calculations consider terrain obstruction, astronomical positions and observation height. Results are displayed as interactive charts and timelines.

4. Mission Windows

Users can choose mission dates and explore estimated periods when selected sunlight and communication-visibility requirements are satisfied.

This helps users understand how changing dates, locations and mission requirements can influence potential operating windows.

5. Mission Brief

The platform generates a summary of the selected location, environmental conditions and mission-window estimates. Users can print or save this information as a PDF using their browser.

Technology and Development

We developed Lunar Mission Navigator using Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS.

For the interactive experience, we used Three.js and React Three Fiber to build the 3D Moon. Motion provides interface animations, while Recharts supports data visualisation.

Our scientific data preparation uses Python scripts to process lunar elevation data, generate terrain-horizon profiles and prepare ephemeris information. The application reads preprocessed datasets directly in the browser rather than relying on a live scientific API.

We also implemented data validation and automated checks to improve consistency and reproducibility.

NASA Data and Scientific Resources

Our project uses lunar terrain information from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), imagery from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), and Sun and Earth position information from NASA/JPL Horizons.

These resources allow us to combine real lunar observations and astronomical ephemerides with estimated terrain-dependent visibility calculations.

The resulting operating windows are educational estimates, not validated engineering predictions or official NASA landing-site assessments.

Creativity and Innovation

Our project's main innovation is combining immersive lunar exploration with interactive environmental analysis.

Instead of presenting scientific information only through static charts or technical datasets, Lunar Mission Navigator allows users to explore the Moon in 3D, change mission dates, compare locations and understand the consequences of different planning assumptions.

Our approach makes the relationship between lunar terrain, sunlight, Earth visibility and mission requirements more intuitive.

Intended Impact

We aim to make space exploration and lunar mission-planning concepts more accessible to students, educators, researchers and space enthusiasts.

The platform demonstrates how openly available NASA datasets can be transformed into educational tools that encourage scientific curiosity, data-driven thinking and an understanding of real exploration challenges.

In the future, the platform could be extended with additional locations, more detailed environmental models and improved mission-planning capabilities.

Limitations

The application is an independent educational prototype. Terrain resolution, approximate location coordinates, horizon modelling and hourly ephemeris sampling introduce uncertainty. Our outputs should not be used for actual spacecraft landing decisions or mission operations.
